extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers seeking an encyclopedic overview of the American Enterprise Institute (AEI)
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia entry describing the American Enterprise Institute's history, research programs, policy positions, funding, criticisms, and institutional activities. The page summarizes AEI program foci, notable scholars, publications, funding sources, and external evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wikipedia sourcing requirement (avoid excessive primary sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: This section relies excessively on references to primary sources. Please improve this section by adding secondary or tertiary sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template appears repeatedly (Area studies; International organizations and economic development; Health policy studies; Legal and constitutional studies; Political and public opinion studies; Social and cultural studies; Education). Actionable guidance: find and add secondary/tertiary sources (news, books, JSTOR, scholarly sources) to replace or supplement primary-source references. The page includes the 'Find sources' helper text and instructions on when to remove the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign and defense policy studies focus
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's foreign and defense policy studies researchers focus on "how political and economic freedom—as well as American interests—are best promoted around the world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrasing defines the program's mission/orienting criterion for evaluating research: emphasis on promoting political/economic freedom and U.S. interests. Use this as a lens to judge whether foreign/defense outputs align with AEI's stated orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy orientation: hard U.S. line on threats
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI staff have tended to be advocates of a hard U.S. line on threats or potential threats to the United States, including (examples) the Soviet Union, Iraq, China, North Korea, Iran, Syria, Venezuela, Russia, and militant groups like al Qaeda and Hezbollah.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes a recurring policy stance used to characterize AEI work; reviewers can use it as a criterion to assess whether specific AEI outputs reflect a hawkish or interventionist posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with neoconservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's foreign and defense policy studies department... is the part of the institute most commonly associated with neoconservatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an ideological/label criterion: external observers often evaluate AEI foreign-policy work through the lens of neoconservative affiliation and personnel (e.g., Richard Perle, Gary Schmitt, Paul Wolfowitz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iraq strategy criteria (Choosing Victory plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AEI report Choosing Victory: A Plan for Success in Iraq called for 'clearing and holding' neighborhoods, securing the population, a troop escalation of seven Army brigades and Marine regiments, and renewed emphasis on reconstruction, economic development, and jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specifies concrete policy prescriptions promoted by AEI researchers; it serves as an evaluative standard for AEI’s Iraq-related policy proposals (e.g., emphasis on counterinsurgency tactics, troop increases, and reconstruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense policy research topics and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's defense policy researchers work on issues related to the U.S. military forces' size and structure and military partnerships with allies (both bilaterally and through institutions such as NATO). Schmitt directs AEI's Program on Advanced Strategic Studies, which 'analyzes the long-term issues that will impact America's security and its ability to lead internationally.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program-level criterion: evaluate outputs on whether they address force structure, alliance management, and long-term strategic challenges consistent with AEI's stated agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area studies program coverage (Asia focus example)
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's Asia studies program covers 'the rise of China as an economic and political power; Taiwan's security and economic agenda; Japan's military transformation; the threat of a nuclear North Korea; and the impact of regional alliances and rivalries on U.S. military and economic relationships in Asia.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lists topical boundaries for the Asia program; use these topics to judge whether AEI Asia outputs fall within the program's stated scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic development research focus and institutional fixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's research on economic development dates back to the early days of the institute; AEI sponsors the Henry Wendt Lecture in International Development; Nicholas Eberstadt holds the Henry Wendt Chair, focusing on demographics, population growth and human capital development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic criterion: assess development research by presence of sustained themes (demographics, human capital) and recurring institutional outputs (lectures, chairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Health policy research focus areas
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's long-term focuses in health care have included national insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, pharmaceutical innovation, health care competition, and cost control. AEI published the Health Policy Outlook series and produced A Better Prescription advocating market-based reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these topics to evaluate AEI health-policy work. The page also documents individual scholars' positions (e.g., Roger Bate, Scott Gottlieb, Robert B. Helms) which show topical emphases and policy prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health policy normative stance: market-based, consumer control
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's A Better Prescription called for putting the money and control in the hands of the consumers and continuing the market-based system of healthcare, 'a form of healthcare that "relies on financial incentives rather than central direction and control."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses a normative criterion for AEI policy proposals: preference for market mechanisms and consumer-directed incentives over centralized plans. Use this to characterize AEI recommendations and judge consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and constitutional studies organization and emphases
rubrics_metrics.description: The AEI Legal Center for the Public Interest (formed in 2007) houses legal and constitutional research. The institute was influential in the law and economics movement and sponsors the annual Gauer Distinguished Lecture in Law and Public Policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic criterion: legal scholarship at AEI is evaluated by its institutional vehicles (Legal Center, lectures) and by named focuses (law & economics, constitutional themes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual legal scholars' research foci
rubrics_metrics.description: Ted Frank focuses on liability law and tort reform. Michael S. Greve focuses on constitutional law and federalism, including federal preemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are example-level criteria for assessing AEI legal outputs: identify which subfields (liability/tort reform, federalism/preemption) the scholar or publication addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and public opinion research activities
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's research program has published studies on political processes and institutions since the 1970s, produced the 'At the Polls' series assessing elections, monitored plebiscites (Palau, Federated States of Micronesia, Marshall Islands), and published Public Opinion magazine (1978–1990).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation metric: outputs include election studies, monitoring reports, magazine/publication series — use these as indicators of program activity and expertise in public opinion research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and cultural studies scope and lecture series
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's social and cultural studies program sponsors research on education, religion, race and gender, and social welfare, and (supported by the Bradley Foundation) has hosted the Bradley Lecture Series since 1989 with notable speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic and output-oriented criterion: scope defined by topics listed and prominence measured by distinguished lecture speakers; use both to evaluate program impact and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education policy studies leadership and positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Education policy studies at AEI are directed by Frederick M. Hess. AEI co-directs the Future of American Education Project and is a national allied organization of the American Federation for Children; it supported Betsy DeVos's positions and criticized the Borrower Defense Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation criteria include leadership, project affiliations, and policy positions (school choice, regulatory positions). Use these to assess AEI's education policy orientation and advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding sources: historical and named donors
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1980s about 60% of funding came from foundations (Lilly Endowment, Smith Richardson Foundation, Rockefeller Brothers Trust, Earhart Foundation) and remaining from corporations (Bethlehem Steel, Exxon, J.C. Penney, Chase Manhattan). Later disclosures include $960,000 from ExxonMobil (as of 2005), Purdue Pharma donations ($50,000/year 2003–2019; >$800,000 total), Donors Capital Fund ($2,000,000 in 2009 tax year), Paul Singer ($1,100,000), Kern Family Foundation ($1,071,912), TECRO, US Chamber of Commerce, Koch-associated foundations, and others. A 2013 study noted $86.7 million between 2003 and 2010.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding is a major evaluative dimension for AEI. The page provides specific donor names and amounts — use these to assess potential influence, funding concentration, and transparency. The entry compiles multiple historical data points provided on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial metrics: revenues and expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI's revenues for the fiscal year ending June 2015 were $84,616,388 against expenses of $38,611,315.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these balance-sheet numbers as quantitative indicators of organizational scale, surplus/deficit, and resource capacity in a given fiscal year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity/evaluator rating
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2014, the charity evaluating service American Institute of Philanthropy gave AEI an 'A−' grade in its CharityWatch 'Top-Rated Charities' listing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party evaluations (charity-watch grades, rankings) are explicit external metrics for judging AEI's financial stewardship and charitable status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think-tank rankings and thematic scores
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI appears in Global Go To Think Tank Report rankings with positions across categories (e.g., Top Think Tank overall and specialized ranks such as Security and International Affairs #32, Health Policy #3, Domestic Economic Policy #10, International Economic Policy #9, Social Policy #7; special achievement categories including Most Innovative Policy Ideas/Proposals #13, Greatest Impact on Public Policy (Global) #13, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rankings across subject categories and 'special achievement' metrics provide multi-dimensional external measures of influence, innovation, media use, and policy impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly and publication outputs (AEI Press, series, reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: AEI has published AEI Press books and series (e.g., Transition Costs of Fundamental Tax Reform; Toward Fundamental Tax Reform; Tax Policy Lessons from the 2000s), AEI Press monographs and reports (e.g., Choosing Victory), and hosted research highlights and lecture series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication series, monographs, and report authorship are program outputs used to evaluate AEI's research productivity and topical contributions; look for recurring series, named reports, and published books as indicators.
